text:
A: Hi. Gareth. Can you hear me?
B: Yeah, fine. Daniel. Nice to meet you.
A: You too. Where are you?
B: Worthing.
A: Ah, south coast. I'm Maidstone. Practically the same road, apart from the A27 being a nightmare.
B: [laughs] Yeah, it always is.
A: I'll be honest, from your photo I put you down as being in the trade. Was I right?
B: Sort of, yeah. I run the trade counter at a builders' merchant in Lancing. Timber, plasterboard, drainage bits. Half six start.
A: Drainage bits! That's me. I'm a civil engineer, drainage and flood risk. So I'm probably the one specifying the stuff your lot can't get in stock.
B: [laughs] You're the reason I get the phone calls, then. Some contractor ringing at seven wanting two hundred metres of a pipe nobody's heard of.
A: Probably, yeah. Sorry about that.
B: No, it's fine. It's the ones who order the wrong sheet sizes I can't stand. Had a bloke in last week, third time he'd done it. I measured it for him in the end.
A: Fair play. And I noticed the books behind you. History?
B: Yeah. I'm doing an Open University module, British social history. Evenings and weekends. Slow going, but I enjoy it.
A: Nice. I'm a podcast man, mostly. I've just listened to one on the Tay Bridge disaster. Eighteen seventy-nine, the whole middle section came down in a storm with a train on it. And the thing is, the engineer had more or less not accounted for wind loading. Which, as an engineer, you listen to and think, yeah, that's the nightmare, that's the one that keeps you up.
B: I think I've heard that one. Was it the one with the Victorian inquiry bit?
A: That's it, yeah.
B: Do you listen to the ones on the First World War at all? I went to Ypres with my dad last year, the war graves. It sort of got to me more than I expected.
A: In what way?
B: Erm, I think just the scale of it. Row after row. And my great-grandfather was out there, so we went looking for his regiment's bit. You stand at the Menin Gate at eight o'clock for the Last Post, and my dad's not a crier, but he went quiet for a good while.
A: Yeah. I can imagine.
B: Do you get on with your dad?
A: Yeah, we go to Charlton together. Three or four times a season. He's had a stroke, couple of years back, so it's a bit slower getting to the ground now. But we still go.
B: Sorry to hear that.
A: No, he's alright. Stubborn. What about football, do you follow anyone?
B: Brighton. Go to the Amex with my dad a few times a season.
A: Ah, well, you've got it good at the minute.
B: Better than it was, yeah. I play five-a-side Wednesdays as well.
A: Wednesdays! Me too. Work lot.
B: Are you any good?
A: I'm told I'm surprisingly competitive. I don't see it myself.
B: [laughs] We're not competitive at all. We just sort of run about and go for a pint.
A: That's the right attitude. I coach my lad's under-tens on a Saturday. They lost seven-one last week and nobody minded.
B: Seven-one. That's—
